AbstractText.Label: BACKGROUND
AbstractText.content: Patients frequently consult primary care physicians and gastroenterologists when experiencing chronic abdominal pain. Although its diagnostic efficacy in these settings is uncertain, small-bowel capsule endoscopy (SBCE) has been used to evaluate the unexplained reasons for abdominal pain.

AbstractText.Label: OBJECTIVE
AbstractText.content: To evaluate the diagnostic yield of SBCE in patients with unexplained chronic abdominal pain.

AbstractText.Label: DESIGN
AbstractText.content: We performed a retrospective review of publications reporting the diagnostic yield of SBCE in patients with unexplained chronic abdominal pain and calculated the overall diagnostic yield.

AbstractText.Label: SETTING
AbstractText.content: Two investigators independently searched studies from databases and analyzed the results.

AbstractText.Label: PATIENTS
AbstractText.content: A total of 1520 patients from 21 studies were included.

AbstractText.Label: MAIN OUTCOME MEASUREMENTS
AbstractText.content: Per-patient diagnostic yield, with 95% confidence intervals (CI), was evaluated by a random-effect model. Clear categorical analysis also was performed.

AbstractText.Label: RESULTS
AbstractText.content: The pooled diagnostic yield of SBCE in patients with unexplained chronic abdominal pain was 20.9% (95% CI, 15.9%-25.9%), with high heterogeneity (I(2) = 80.0%; P ＜ .001). Inflammatory lesions were the most common (78.3%) positive findings, followed by tumors (9.0%).

AbstractText.Label: LIMITATIONS
AbstractText.content: Heterogeneity among studies, retrospective design, variable chronicity of abdominal pain, and different previous examinations before SBCE.

AbstractText.Label: CONCLUSION
AbstractText.content: SBCE provides a noninvasive diagnostic tool for patients with unexplained chronic abdominal pain, but the diagnostic yield is limited (20.9%). Among patients with positive findings, inflammatory lesions are the most common.
